question.scenario: You need to grant a specific user read access to all objects in a single Cloud Storage bucket without giving access to other buckets.
question.question-text: At which level should you grant the IAM role?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: IAM permissions are inherited downward through the resource hierarchy. Grant at the most specific level that covers the access needed without granting broader access than required.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Grant the roles/storage.objectViewer role at the bucket level (B) to provide read access to all objects within that specific bucket without affecting other buckets. IAM permissions are inherited, so a bucket-level binding automatically applies to every object in the bucket. Object-level permissions (A) would work but require granting access to each object individually, which is impractical and does not cover future objects. Project-level (D) and organization-level (C) grants would give access to all buckets in the project or organization respectively, violating the requirement to limit access to a single bucket.

ul.li: Uniform bucket-level access (enabled by default on new buckets) disables object-level ACLs and enforces IAM-only permissions. This simplifies access management and ensures consistent authorization semantics. When enabled, all access is controlled through IAM bindings at the bucket or higher level, not per-object ACLs.

Project-level storage roles (e.g., roles/storage.objectViewer at the project level) grant access to all buckets and their objects in the project. This is overly permissive when only one bucket needs to be shared. Always scope storage IAM bindings to the bucket level for single-bucket access requirements.

IAM Conditions allow even more granular control within a bucket-level binding. For example, you can grant access only during business hours, only to objects with a specific prefix (simulating folder-level access), or only from specific IP ranges using attribute-based conditions in the role binding.

For temporary access needs, use signed URLs instead of IAM bindings. A signed URL grants time-limited read or write access to a specific object without requiring the requester to have any IAM role, which is useful for sharing individual files with external users who do not have Google Cloud accounts.

question.title: Secret Management
question.scenario: Your application needs to access database credentials and API keys securely without storing them in code or configuration files.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service should you use to manage these secrets?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Google Cloud has a purpose-built service for storing, versioning, and securely delivering sensitive values like passwords, API keys, and certificates to applications at runtime.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Secret Manager (B) is Google Cloud's purpose-built service for storing and managing sensitive data. It provides automatic encryption at rest, IAM-based access control, secret versioning, audit logging of all access, and rotation scheduling. Cloud KMS (A) manages encryption keys used to encrypt/decrypt data but does not store the secrets themselves. Cloud Storage with encryption (C) stores files securely but lacks secret-specific features like versioning, rotation, and access auditing. Environment variables in Cloud Run (D) store values in plaintext in the service configuration, visible to anyone with the Service Viewer role, and do not provide versioning or rotation.

ul.li: Secret Manager stores secrets as versioned byte strings. Each version is immutable once created, and you can access specific versions or the "latest" alias. Applications call the Secret Manager API to retrieve secret values at runtime, keeping secrets out of code repositories, container images, and environment variable configurations.

Cloud KMS is complementary to Secret Manager, not a replacement. KMS manages cryptographic keys for encrypting/decrypting arbitrary data, signing/verifying, and wrapping other keys. Secret Manager can use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) from Cloud KMS to encrypt secret data at rest, combining both services for defense in depth.

Cloud Run and Cloud Functions have native Secret Manager integration: mount secrets as environment variables or file volumes directly in the service configuration. The platform handles fetching the secret value at container startup, so your code reads a regular environment variable or file without needing Secret Manager client library calls.

Grant the Secret Manager Secret Accessor role (roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor) to the application's service account for least-privilege access. This role allows reading secret values but not creating, deleting, or modifying secrets. Combine with Data Access audit logs to track which identity accessed which secret and when.

question.title: Identity-Aware Proxy
question.scenario: You need to provide secure access to an internal web application for employees without setting up a VPN. Access should be based on user identity and context.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service enables this zero-trust access model?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Google's zero-trust access service verifies user identity and device context before allowing access to applications, replacing traditional VPN-based perimeter security.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Identity-Aware Proxy (A) implements a zero-trust security model by verifying user identity (via Google sign-in) and evaluating context (device security status, IP address, time of day) before granting access to applications. It sits in front of your application as a reverse proxy, intercepting every request and checking authorization against IAM policies. Cloud VPN (B) creates an encrypted tunnel but uses network-based perimeter security, not identity-based access. Cloud Load Balancing with SSL (C) handles traffic distribution and encryption but does not authenticate individual users. Cloud Armor (D) provides DDoS protection and WAF rules but does not perform identity verification.

ul.li: IAP integrates with App Engine, Cloud Run, Compute Engine (behind an HTTPS load balancer), and GKE. For Compute Engine, IAP acts as an authenticating reverse proxy: users hit the load balancer, IAP verifies their Google identity and IAM permissions (roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor), and only authorized requests reach the backend VMs.

IAP also supports TCP forwarding for SSH and RDP access to VMs without external IP addresses. Using gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap routes the SSH connection through IAP, which authenticates the user with their Google identity and checks the IAP-secured Tunnel User role before allowing the connection.

Access levels in Access Context Manager define context-aware conditions: trusted device certificates, allowed IP ranges, allowed geographic regions, and required device management status. IAP evaluates these access levels alongside IAM roles, enabling policies like "allow access only from managed corporate devices on the corporate network."

IAP implements Google's BeyondCorp zero-trust security model, which shifts access controls from the network perimeter to individual users and devices. This means employees can access internal applications from any network (home, cafe, airport) as long as their identity and device context satisfy the configured access policy.

question.title: Organization Policies
question.scenario: Your security team wants to prevent anyone in the organization from creating Compute Engine instances with external IP addresses.
question.question-text: Which feature should you use to enforce this restriction?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Organization policies constrain how resources can be configured across the entire organization, independent of IAM permissions. They enforce guardrails that even administrators cannot bypass.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: An organization policy constraint (A) is the correct tool. The compute.vmExternalIpAccess constraint prevents VMs from being assigned external IP addresses regardless of the user's IAM permissions. This is enforced at the resource creation level, meaning even an Owner cannot create a VM with an external IP when this constraint is active. IAM deny policies (B) block specific permissions but are harder to maintain for this use case. VPC firewall rules (C) control network traffic but do not prevent the assignment of external IPs. Custom IAM roles (D) could omit certain permissions but are easily bypassed by granting additional roles.

ul.li: Organization policies are fundamentally different from IAM. IAM controls who can perform actions (authentication and authorization), while organization policies control what resource configurations are allowed. Even a user with the Owner role is subject to organization policy constraints, making them a stronger enforcement mechanism for security guardrails.

The compute.vmExternalIpAccess constraint is a list constraint that specifies which VMs (by full resource name) are allowed to have external IPs. Setting the constraint to deny all at the organization level and then allowing specific exceptions at the project or folder level enables a default-deny posture with controlled exceptions.

Organization policies are inherited down the resource hierarchy (Organization > Folder > Project) and can be overridden at lower levels if the Organization Policy Administrator role is granted. Use hierarchical inheritance strategically: set restrictive defaults at the organization level and grant exceptions at lower levels only when justified.

Test organization policies before enforcement using the Policy Simulator or by applying them to a test folder first. Review the Organization Policy service logs in Cloud Audit Logs to identify which resource creation attempts would be denied, then create necessary exceptions before enforcing organization-wide.

question.title: Private Google Access
question.scenario: Your VM instances have no external IP addresses but need to access Google Cloud APIs and services like Cloud Storage.
question.question-text: Which feature enables these VMs to access Google APIs privately?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A subnet-level setting allows VMs with only internal IP addresses to reach Google Cloud API endpoints through Google's internal network without requiring external IPs or NAT.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Private Google Access (C) enables VM instances with only internal IP addresses to communicate with Google APIs and services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub, etc.) through Google's internal network. It is enabled per subnet and requires no additional infrastructure. Cloud NAT (B) provides outbound internet access for VMs without external IPs, which could technically reach Google APIs via the public internet, but it is not the intended or recommended solution for Google API access. VPC peering (A) connects two VPC networks privately but does not provide access to Google APIs. Cloud Interconnect (D) connects on-premises networks to Google Cloud, not internal VMs to Google APIs.

ul.li: Enable Private Google Access on a subnet with gcloud compute networks subnets update SUBNET --enable-private-ip-google-access --region=REGION. Traffic from VMs in that subnet to Google API endpoints (*.googleapis.com) is routed through Google's internal network without traversing the public internet, improving security and reducing egress costs.

Cloud NAT provides outbound internet connectivity for VMs without external IPs by performing network address translation at the VPC level. While VMs behind Cloud NAT can reach Google APIs through the public internet, this is less secure and less efficient than Private Google Access, which keeps traffic entirely within Google's network.

Private Service Connect extends the Private Google Access concept by creating private endpoints (internal IP addresses within your VPC) for specific Google APIs. This gives you DNS-level control, firewall rule targeting, and VPC Service Controls integration, providing more granular security than standard Private Google Access.

Combine Private Google Access with VPC Service Controls for maximum data security. Private Google Access ensures API traffic stays on Google's internal network, while VPC Service Controls prevent data exfiltration through those APIs. Together they create a strong security posture for sensitive workloads that must not expose data to the public internet.

question.title: Audit Logging
question.scenario: Your compliance team needs to track who accessed sensitive data in BigQuery and what queries they ran.
question.question-text: Which type of Cloud Audit Log captures this information?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Audit Logs are split into four types based on what they capture. The type that records API calls reading or modifying user-provided data is the one needed for tracking data access and queries.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Data Access audit logs (C) capture API calls that read user data (DATA_READ), write user data (DATA_WRITE), and list/get resource metadata (ADMIN_READ). For BigQuery, this includes every query execution, showing who ran which query, on which datasets, and when. Admin Activity logs (B) record configuration changes like creating or deleting resources, not data reads. System Event logs (D) capture Google-initiated system actions such as live migrations. Policy Denied logs (A) record access attempts blocked by VPC Service Controls or organization policies. Data Access logs must be explicitly enabled for most services as they can generate high volume, though BigQuery has them enabled by default.

ul.li: Admin Activity audit logs are always enabled, cannot be disabled, are retained for 400 days at no charge, and record all API calls that modify resource configuration (create, delete, update operations). They answer "who changed what" but not "who read what data."

Data Access audit logs are disabled by default for most services due to their high volume and associated storage costs. BigQuery is a notable exception: its Data Access logs are enabled by default. For other services, enable them via the IAM & Admin audit logs configuration page or gcloud projects set-iam-policy with the auditLogConfigs section.

Data Access logs for BigQuery include the full SQL query text in the metadata field, making them invaluable for compliance audits. You can see exactly which tables were queried, by which principal, from which IP address, and at what timestamp, providing a complete access trail for sensitive data.

System Event audit logs record automated actions performed by Google systems, such as Compute Engine live migrations, auto-scaling events, and scheduled maintenance. They are always on and free, but they track infrastructure operations, not user-initiated data access, making them irrelevant for data access compliance tracking.

question.title: Cloud Shell Usage
question.scenario: A team member needs to run gcloud commands but cannot install the Cloud SDK on their corporate laptop due to IT restrictions.
question.question-text: What is the recommended alternative for accessing gcloud tools?

choices.choice: Request IT to whitelist the SDK installation
Use Cloud Shell in the Google Cloud Console
Use the REST API directly with curl
Install the SDK in a Docker container

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Google Cloud Console includes a browser-based shell environment with all CLI tools pre-installed, requiring no local software installation beyond a web browser.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Shell (B) is the recommended alternative because it provides a fully configured command-line environment directly in the browser, requiring no local installation. It includes gcloud, kubectl, gsutil, docker, terraform, and other commonly used tools pre-installed and automatically updated. Cloud Shell authenticates with the user's Google Cloud identity, so there is no credential configuration needed. Using the REST API with curl (C) is technically possible but requires manual authentication token management and is impractical for daily operations. Docker (D) and IT whitelisting (A) both require local installation permissions the user does not have.

ul.li: Cloud Shell runs on a temporary e2-small Compute Engine VM (0.5 vCPU, 2 GB RAM) in a Google-managed project. It provisions within seconds on first use, provides Debian-based Linux with root access via sudo, and includes 5 GB of persistent home directory storage backed by a persistent disk that survives session timeouts.

Sessions automatically terminate after 20 minutes of inactivity (no keyboard/mouse input) and after a maximum continuous use of 12 hours. The underlying VM is ephemeral: only the /home directory persists. Installed packages, files outside /home, and running processes are lost when the session ends.

Cloud Shell Editor is a built-in web-based IDE (based on Theia/VS Code) accessible from Cloud Shell for editing files, browsing the file system, and managing Git repositories. It provides IntelliSense, syntax highlighting, and integrated terminal, making it suitable for light development and configuration tasks.

Cloud Shell has built-in web preview functionality that creates a temporary proxy to expose ports 8080-8084 from the Cloud Shell VM to your browser. This allows testing web applications, APIs, and other services running in Cloud Shell without configuring firewall rules or external access.

question.title: Hybrid Connectivity
question.scenario: Your company needs a dedicated, high-bandwidth, low-latency connection between your on-premises data center and Google Cloud for large data transfers.
question.question-text: Which connectivity option provides dedicated physical connectivity?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Only one connectivity option provides a direct physical cross-connect between your network equipment and Google's network at a colocation facility, without any third-party provider in between.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Dedicated Interconnect (C) provides direct physical connections between your on-premises network and Google's network at a supported colocation facility. It offers 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps links with SLA-backed availability and reduced egress pricing compared to internet-based options. Partner Interconnect (A) provides similar private connectivity but through a supported service provider, meaning the physical link is managed by a third party, not your own equipment. Cloud VPN (B) creates encrypted tunnels over the public internet, which introduces shared-bandwidth variability and higher latency. Direct Peering (D) connects your network to Google's edge for Google service traffic but does not provide access to your VPC network and has no SLA.

ul.li: Dedicated Interconnect requires your network equipment to be physically present in a supported colocation facility where Google has a point of presence. You provision a physical cross-connect (fiber patch) between your router and Google's peering router, establishing a direct Layer 2 link with no shared infrastructure.

Partner Interconnect is the alternative when you cannot meet Google at a colocation facility. A supported service provider (e.g., Equinix, Megaport, PacketFabric) provisions the physical connectivity, and you get a VLAN attachment to your VPC. Bandwidth options range from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps depending on the partner.

Cloud VPN tunnels (Classic VPN or HA VPN) encrypt traffic using IPsec and route it over the public internet. HA VPN provides 99.99% availability with two tunnels across two interfaces. While suitable for modest bandwidth needs (up to 3 Gbps per tunnel), VPN cannot match Interconnect's throughput or latency consistency for large data transfers.

For maximum availability, deploy redundant Dedicated Interconnect connections in two different colocation facilities (metro-level redundancy). Google offers a 99.99% SLA for this topology. A single facility with redundant connections provides 99.9% SLA. VLAN attachments (Interconnect Attachments) bridge the physical Interconnect link to your VPC's Cloud Router for BGP-based dynamic routing.

question.title: GKE Cluster Creation
question.scenario: You need to create a GKE cluster that automatically manages node upgrades and scales the node pool based on workload demands.
question.question-text: Which flags should you include when creating the cluster?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GKE Standard clusters expose three separate node management features as individual flags: autoscaling adjusts node count, autoupgrade handles version updates, and autorepair replaces unhealthy nodes.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The correct flags are --enable-autoscaling, --enable-autorepair, and --enable-autoupgrade (A). These are distinct GKE Standard cluster features: autoscaling adjusts the number of nodes in a node pool based on pending pod scheduling demands, autoupgrade automatically updates nodes to newer Kubernetes versions following the release channel schedule, and autorepair detects and recreates nodes that fail health checks. Options B and C use fabricated flag names that do not exist in the gcloud container CLI. Option D (--autopilot-mode) would create a GKE Autopilot cluster, which manages all infrastructure automatically but was not what the question asked for.

ul.li: Cluster autoscaling monitors for pods in Pending state (cannot be scheduled due to insufficient node resources) and adds nodes to the pool until all pods can be scheduled or the max node count is reached. Conversely, it removes underutilized nodes when their pods can be rescheduled elsewhere, scaling down during low-demand periods to save costs.

Autoupgrade follows the cluster's release channel (Rapid, Regular, or Stable) to determine when nodes are upgraded. Nodes are drained gracefully (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets) and replaced with nodes running the new version. Maintenance windows and exclusions can restrict when upgrades occur to avoid business-critical periods.

Autorepair monitors node health using periodic health checks. If a node reports NotReady status for approximately 10 minutes, or if its boot disk is unhealthy, autorepair drains the node and recreates it from the node pool's instance template. This automatic remediation prevents degraded cluster capacity from accumulating over time.

GKE Autopilot (--cluster-version and mode=autopilot) abstracts away all node management: Google manages nodes, auto-repairs, auto-upgrades, and auto-scales transparently. You only define pod-level resource requests, and Autopilot provisions exactly the infrastructure needed. It is simpler but offers less control over node configuration than Standard clusters with these three flags.

question.title: Preemptible VM Management
question.scenario: Your batch processing jobs can tolerate interruptions. You want to reduce compute costs by using preemptible VMs but need to handle terminations gracefully.
question.question-text: What is the maximum duration a preemptible VM can run before automatic termination?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Preemptible VMs have a hard maximum runtime enforced by Google Cloud, after which they are automatically terminated regardless of workload status or resource availability.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Preemptible VMs are automatically terminated after a maximum of 24 hours (C) of continuous runtime. In addition to this hard time limit, they can be preempted at any time if Google Cloud needs the capacity for on-demand workloads. Despite these limitations, preemptible VMs offer 60-91% cost savings compared to on-demand pricing, making them ideal for batch processing, data analysis, and other fault-tolerant workloads. The 7-day (A), 12-hour (B), and 1-hour (D) options are all incorrect maximum durations.

ul.li: When a preemptible VM is about to be terminated (either at the 24-hour limit or due to capacity reclamation), Compute Engine sends a preemption notice via the instance metadata endpoint and an ACPI G2 soft-off signal. The VM has approximately 30 seconds to perform graceful shutdown tasks before being forcibly terminated.

Use shutdown scripts (--metadata shutdown-script=SCRIPT) to handle graceful termination: checkpoint processing state to Cloud Storage or a persistent disk, flush in-memory buffers, and deregister from load balancers. Design batch jobs with checkpointing so they can resume from the last checkpoint on a new instance.

Spot VMs (--provisioning-model=SPOT) are the successor to preemptible VMs. They offer the same pricing discounts but without the 24-hour maximum runtime limit. Spot VMs can still be preempted at any time for capacity reasons, but they will run indefinitely if capacity remains available, making them strictly superior for long-running fault-tolerant workloads.

Preemptible and Spot VMs are not covered by any Compute Engine SLA and cannot live-migrate during host maintenance events. Use them in managed instance groups with autoscaling to automatically recreate preempted instances, maintaining the desired capacity for batch processing pipelines.

question.title: Custom IAM Roles
question.scenario: You need to create a role that combines specific permissions from multiple predefined roles, following the principle of least privilege.
question.question-text: What type of IAM role should you create?

choices.choice: Custom role with only the required permissions
Service account role with limited scope

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Custom IAM roles let you hand-pick individual permissions from across all Google Cloud services into a single role, granting exactly the access needed and nothing more.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A custom role with only the required permissions (A) is the correct approach. Custom IAM roles allow you to select a precise set of permissions and bundle them into a role tailored to your specific needs. Basic roles (B) are coarse-grained (Viewer, Editor, Owner) and cannot have permissions added to them; they grant broad access across all services. Predefined roles (C) are maintained by Google and cannot be modified or have permissions removed. There is no concept of a "service account role with limited scope" (D) as a distinct role type; service accounts use the same IAM roles as other principals.

ul.li: Create custom roles at the project or organization level using gcloud iam roles create ROLE_ID --project=PROJECT --permissions=PERMISSION1,PERMISSION2 or with a YAML definition file. Organization-level custom roles can be granted on any resource within the organization, while project-level roles can only be used within that project.

Not all permissions are available for custom roles. Some permissions are marked as NOT_APPLICABLE or TESTING and cannot be included. Use gcloud iam list-testable-permissions to check which permissions can be used in custom roles for a given resource level, and review the "Custom roles support" column in the IAM permissions reference documentation.

Custom roles require ongoing maintenance. When Google launches new features or services, new permissions are added to predefined roles automatically, but custom roles must be manually updated to include newly created permissions. Set up a review process to periodically compare your custom roles against the predefined roles they were derived from.

Use IAM Recommender to identify which permissions are actually being used by principals. Start by granting a predefined role, let the Recommender observe usage for 90 days, then create a custom role containing only the permissions that were actually exercised. This data-driven approach ensures the custom role is both least-privilege and functional.

question.title: Region and Zone Selection
question.scenario: You are deploying an application that must comply with data residency requirements mandating that data remain within the European Union.
question.question-text: How should you approach region selection?

choices.choice: Use any region and enable data encryption
Select regions located within the EU, such as europe-west1 or europe-west4
Deploy globally and use VPN to restrict access
Use multi-regional storage with EU location

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Data residency compliance requires physically locating resources in the required jurisdiction. Encryption and access controls do not change where data is physically stored.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Selecting EU-located regions like europe-west1 (Belgium) or europe-west4 (Netherlands) (B) ensures that compute and storage resources physically reside within the European Union. Using any region with encryption (A) does not satisfy residency requirements because the data physically exists outside the EU regardless of encryption. Deploying globally with VPN (C) still places data in non-EU regions. Multi-regional EU storage (D) keeps data within the EU but only addresses storage, not the compute, database, and other resources that also process and hold data subject to residency rules.

ul.li: Enforce data residency at the organizational level using the gcp.resourceLocations organization policy constraint. Set the allowed values to EU regions only (in:eu-locations), which prevents anyone in the organization from creating resources in non-EU regions, providing a guardrail that survives individual project misconfigurations.

Data residency applies to data at rest and data in processing, not just storage. Consider all services that handle regulated data: Cloud SQL instances, GKE clusters, Pub/Sub message storage, Dataflow processing jobs, and temporary data in Cloud Build. All must be deployed in EU regions to maintain compliance.

Multi-regional Cloud Storage with the EU location type stores data redundantly across multiple EU regions but never outside the EU. This is suitable for storage-only residency but does not cover compute resources. For full compliance, combine EU multi-regional storage with EU regional compute deployments.

Google Cloud's EU data boundary commitments are documented in the Data Processing Addendum and regional data processing terms. Review the specific Google Cloud services compliance page to confirm which services support EU data residency, as some managed services may process metadata or control plane data outside the selected region.

question.title: Cloud Pub/Sub Integration
question.scenario: You need to build an event-driven architecture where multiple services consume the same messages independently at their own pace.
question.question-text: How should you configure Cloud Pub/Sub to support this pattern?

choices.choice: Create multiple topics, one per consuming service
Use pull delivery with a single subscription and distribute messages manually
Create one subscription shared across all services
Create one topic with multiple subscriptions, one per consuming service

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: In Pub/Sub's fan-out pattern, each subscription to a topic receives an independent copy of every published message, allowing multiple consumers to process the same events independently.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: One topic with multiple subscriptions (D) implements the fan-out messaging pattern. Each subscription receives a copy of every message published to the topic, and each consuming service processes messages from its own subscription at its own pace. A shared subscription (C) distributes messages among subscribers using load balancing, meaning each message goes to only one consumer, not all consumers. Multiple topics (A) would require the publisher to send to each topic, adding complexity and coupling. A single subscription with manual distribution (B) defeats the purpose of using Pub/Sub's built-in delivery mechanics and creates a single point of failure.

ul.li: The fan-out pattern (one topic, N subscriptions) ensures each consuming service sees every message independently. Messages remain in each subscription until acknowledged by that subscription's consumer, so a slow consumer does not block others. Pub/Sub retains unacknowledged messages for up to 7 days (configurable with message retention duration).

A shared subscription (multiple consumers pulling from one subscription) implements the competing consumers pattern, where Pub/Sub load-balances messages across the consumers. This is useful for scaling a single service horizontally but is the wrong pattern when multiple different services each need every message.

Dead-letter topics capture messages that fail processing after a configurable number of delivery attempts (max_delivery_attempts). Attach a dead-letter topic to each subscription to prevent poison messages from blocking the subscription. Monitor the dead-letter subscription for investigation and reprocessing of failed messages.

For ordering guarantees, use ordering keys when publishing. Messages with the same ordering key are delivered in order within a subscription. Without ordering keys, Pub/Sub may deliver messages out of order for higher throughput. If your consuming services require strict ordering, design your topic and ordering key strategy before implementation.

question.title: Persistent Disk Types
question.scenario: Your database workload requires high IOPS and low latency storage for optimal performance.
question.question-text: Which persistent disk type should you choose?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Among the network-attached persistent disk options, SSD persistent disks deliver the highest IOPS and lowest latency while still providing durability, snapshots, and resizing capabilities.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SSD persistent disks (pd-ssd) (D) provide the highest IOPS and lowest latency among the network-attached persistent disk types, making them ideal for database workloads that require consistent high performance. While Local SSDs (A) offer even higher raw performance, they are physically attached to the host machine and their data is ephemeral (lost when the VM stops, is preempted, or the host fails), making them unsuitable for database storage that requires durability. Standard persistent disks (pd-standard) (B) use HDD-backed storage with the lowest IOPS and are suited for sequential workloads. Balanced persistent disks (pd-balanced) (C) offer moderate performance at a lower cost than pd-ssd but cannot match pd-ssd for demanding database workloads.

ul.li: pd-ssd delivers up to 100,000 read IOPS and 70,000 write IOPS per instance (depending on disk size and machine type). IOPS and throughput scale linearly with disk size up to the per-instance maximum. For databases that need maximum performance, provision a larger disk even if you do not need all the storage capacity.

pd-balanced provides a good performance-to-cost ratio with up to 80,000 read IOPS and 30,000 write IOPS. It is suitable for general-purpose workloads and boot disks. pd-standard offers only up to 7,500 read IOPS using HDD backing and is best for bulk storage and sequential access patterns like data warehousing.

Local SSDs provide the highest raw performance (up to 2.4 million read IOPS across 24 local SSD partitions) but with critical limitations: data does not survive VM termination, live migration, or host maintenance events. Use them only for temporary storage like caches, scratch space, or replicated data stores where loss of a single node is tolerable.

Persistent disks support online resize (increase size without unmounting), snapshots for backup and cross-region duplication, and multi-reader mode (read-only attachment to multiple VMs simultaneously). These features, combined with built-in redundancy within the zone, make persistent disks the appropriate choice for database storage despite lower raw IOPS than Local SSD.

question.title: Workload Identity
question.scenario: Your GKE pods need to access Cloud Storage and BigQuery. You want to avoid using service account keys and follow security best practices.
question.question-text: Which feature allows GKE pods to authenticate to Google Cloud services without service account keys?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Workload Identity federates Kubernetes service account identity with Google Cloud IAM, allowing pods to authenticate to Google APIs using their Kubernetes identity without any key files.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Workload Identity (B) is the recommended way for GKE workloads to authenticate to Google Cloud services. It creates a trust relationship between a Kubernetes service account (KSA) and a Google Cloud service account (GSA), allowing pods running with that KSA to impersonate the GSA and obtain short-lived access tokens automatically. This eliminates the need to create, distribute, and rotate service account key files. Binary Authorization (A) verifies container image provenance before deployment but does not handle authentication. Pod Security Policies (C, deprecated in favor of Pod Security Standards) control pod-level security constraints. Network Policies (D) control pod-to-pod network traffic but do not address API authentication.

ul.li: Workload Identity setup requires three steps: enable Workload Identity on the cluster (--workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog), annotate the Kubernetes service account with the Google service account email (iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=GSA@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com), and grant the Workload Identity User role on the GSA to the KSA principal (serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA_NAME]).

Without Workload Identity, the common alternative is to mount a service account key file as a Kubernetes secret and set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable. This approach is insecure because key files are long-lived credentials that can be exfiltrated from the cluster and used externally. Workload Identity replaces this with short-lived, automatically rotated tokens.

Applications using Google Cloud client libraries with Application Default Credentials (ADC) work seamlessly with Workload Identity. The GKE metadata server intercepts metadata requests from the pod and returns access tokens for the mapped Google service account, requiring zero code changes in applications already using ADC.

Workload Identity provides pod-level identity isolation: different pods in the same namespace (or even on the same node) can have different Google Cloud service accounts based on their Kubernetes service account annotation. This is more granular than node-level service accounts, where all pods on a node share the same Google Cloud identity.

question.title: Cloud Monitoring Dashboards
question.scenario: Your team needs to visualize key performance metrics for your application including request latency, error rates, and resource utilization in a single view.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Monitoring feature should you use to create this visualization?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Custom dashboards in Cloud Monitoring allow you to arrange multiple metric visualizations (charts, gauges, scorecards) on a single page for comprehensive application observability.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A custom dashboard with multiple charts (C) is the correct feature for creating a unified view of multiple metrics. Dashboards support line charts, stacked area charts, bar charts, heatmaps, gauges, and scorecards, all on a single page with a synchronized time range selector. You can display request latency (p50, p95, p99), error rates (5xx count per minute), and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk) together. Logs Explorer (A) is for searching and browsing log entries, not metric visualization. Alerting policy summaries (B) show alert states but are not customizable metric dashboards. Service monitoring (D) provides SLO-focused views for individual services, not custom multi-metric layouts.

ul.li: Dashboards can be created in the Console UI or defined as JSON and managed as infrastructure-as-code using the Cloud Monitoring API or Terraform google_monitoring_dashboard resource. JSON-based dashboards can be version-controlled in Git, shared across projects via gcloud monitoring dashboards create --config-from-file, and deployed consistently across environments.

MQL (Monitoring Query Language) provides advanced metric querying capabilities within dashboard charts. MQL supports operations like fetch, filter, group_by, align, and outer_join, enabling complex derived metrics such as error rate percentages (errors divided by total requests) directly in the chart configuration without creating separate log-based metrics.

Dashboard widgets include log panels that display recent log entries alongside metric charts, enabling correlation between metric anomalies and log events on the same page. When a latency spike appears in a chart, the adjacent log panel can show corresponding error messages or warnings from the same time window.

Service monitoring provides SLO-based dashboards that track availability and latency against defined objectives (e.g., 99.9% of requests complete within 200ms). While powerful for SRE workflows, it is scoped to individual services with predefined SLI metrics, not the flexible multi-metric layout that custom dashboards provide for general operational visibility.

term.name: Project
term.definition: The fundamental organizational unit in Google Cloud that contains all resources and is the basis for enabling APIs and billing.
term.exam-note: Projects provide resource isolation, billing boundaries, and IAM policies. Each resource belongs to exactly one project.

term.name: Region
term.definition: A specific geographic location where Google Cloud resources are hosted, consisting of multiple zones.
term.exam-note: Choose regions based on latency requirements, data residency, and service availability. Regional resources provide higher availability than zonal.

term.name: Zone
term.definition: An isolated location within a region, providing fault isolation from other zones.
term.exam-note: Zones are independent failure domains. Distribute resources across zones for high availability within a region.

term.name: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
term.definition: A global, private network that spans all regions and provides connectivity for Google Cloud resources.
term.exam-note: VPCs are global but subnets are regional. Use custom mode VPCs for production to control IP ranges.

term.name: Identity and Access Management (IAM)
term.definition: Google Cloud's system for managing authentication and authorization to resources through policies, roles, and permissions.
term.exam-note: IAM follows the principle of least privilege. Policies are additive and inherited down the resource hierarchy.

term.name: Service Account
term.definition: A special account used by applications and services to authenticate and access Google Cloud resources.
term.exam-note: Use custom service accounts with minimal permissions. Avoid default service accounts in production.

term.name: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
term.definition: A managed Kubernetes service for deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications.
term.exam-note: GKE Standard provides node-level control; Autopilot fully manages infrastructure. Use Workload Identity for service authentication.

term.name: Cloud Run
term.definition: A fully managed serverless platform for running stateless containers that automatically scales based on incoming requests.
term.exam-note: Cloud Run scales to zero when idle and charges only for request processing time. Supports any language via containers.

term.name: Cloud Storage
term.definition: Object storage service for storing and retrieving unstructured data with multiple storage classes for different access patterns.
term.exam-note: Choose storage class based on access frequency: Standard, Nearline (monthly), Coldline (quarterly), Archive (yearly).

term.name: Cloud SQL
term.definition: A fully managed relational database service supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server.
term.exam-note: Use REGIONAL availability type for high availability. Supports automatic backups and read replicas.

term.name: Cloud Spanner
term.definition: A globally distributed, strongly consistent relational database service that scales horizontally.
term.exam-note: Spanner provides 99.999% availability with multi-region configs. Use for global applications requiring strong consistency.

term.name: BigQuery
term.definition: A serverless, highly scalable enterprise data warehouse for analytics and machine learning.
term.exam-note: BigQuery separates storage and compute. Use partitioning and clustering to optimize query costs.

term.name: Cloud Logging
term.definition: A fully managed service for storing, searching, analyzing, and alerting on log data.
term.exam-note: Install Ops Agent for application logs. Use log sinks for long-term retention to Cloud Storage or BigQuery.

term.name: Cloud Monitoring
term.definition: A service for collecting metrics, creating dashboards, and setting up alerts for Google Cloud resources.
term.exam-note: Create alerting policies with notification channels. Use uptime checks for endpoint availability monitoring.

term.name: Cloud Build
term.definition: A serverless CI/CD platform for building, testing, and deploying code to Google Cloud.
term.exam-note: Triggers automate builds on repository events. cloudbuild.yaml defines build steps and deployments.

term.name: Artifact Registry
term.definition: A universal package manager for storing and managing container images, language packages, and OS packages.
term.exam-note: Artifact Registry replaces Container Registry. Supports Docker, Maven, npm, Python, and other formats.

term.name: Cloud Functions
term.definition: A serverless execution environment for building event-driven applications with automatic scaling.
term.exam-note: Supports HTTP triggers and event triggers (Pub/Sub, Storage, etc.). 2nd gen uses Cloud Run infrastructure.

term.name: Cloud Pub/Sub
term.definition: A fully managed real-time messaging service for event-driven systems and streaming analytics.
term.exam-note: Messages are delivered to all subscriptions on a topic. Use dead-letter topics for failed message handling.

term.name: Secret Manager
term.definition: A secure service for storing and managing sensitive data like API keys, passwords, and certificates.
term.exam-note: Secrets are versioned and encrypted. Grant Secret Accessor role for applications to read secrets.

term.name: Cloud Load Balancing
term.definition: A fully distributed software-defined load balancing service for distributing traffic across resources.
term.exam-note: Global HTTP(S) LB for multi-region web apps. Components: forwarding rule, target proxy, URL map, backend service.
